common_name: King George Chrysanthemum (Red-and-Yellow Reflex Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; King George is grown as a single disbudded stem in the classic reflex exhibition style.

directions: King George is a reflex-division exhibition chrysanthemum whose downward-curving, overlapping florets build a shaggy, layered mophead bloom in red with a contrasting yellow reverse that flashes as the petals cascade. Pinch the young plant once in late spring to set bud sites, then disbud ruthlessly down to a single terminal flower so all the plant's energy goes into one large, well-formed bloom, staking the stem early since the finished flower head is heavy. Propagate from fresh basal cuttings taken off overwintered stock each late winter rather than dividing old clumps, since this exhibition class is maintained through annual propagation for best bloom quality.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Chrysanthemum Classification Guide

common_name: Samson Chrysanthemum (Deep Red Reflex Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Samson is an early-flowering reflex exhibition type that can be grown either disbudded or in multi-bloom sprays.

directions: Samson is a large-flowered reflex exhibition mum with naturally good form, producing deep red, densely overlapping florets that need comparatively little grooming to look show-ready. It flowers earlier than most exhibition cultivars, finishing its bloom cycle in late September into mid-October, which makes it useful for early shows or for cut-flower growers who want color before the main exhibition season. Grow it as a single disbudded stem for maximum bloom size, or leave side buds in place and grow it as a branching spray for cutting; propagate fresh basal cuttings from stock plants each year rather than relying on an aging clump.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Chrysanthemum Classification Guide

common_name: Mason's Bronze Chrysanthemum (Semi-Double Bronze Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Mason's Bronze forms a tidy, rounded plant rather than the tall single-stem habit of some exhibition types.

directions: Mason's Bronze is a semi-double exhibition-type chrysanthemum with warm bronze-orange flowers and a naturally round, well-filled growth habit. Fertilize every two weeks from midsummer until the buds begin to show color, and stop pinching stem tips by midsummer so the plant has time to set and finish its flowers before fall frost. In cold-winter climates lift and store the crowns after cutting the top growth back to a few inches, or mulch the crowns well in place where winters are milder, and divide plants every couple of years to keep the center of the clump from thinning out.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Chrysanthemum 'Mason's Bronze' Plant Profile
National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Chrysanthemum Classification Guide

common_name: Sam Oldham Chrysanthemum (Crimson Reflex Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after the last frost in full sun and fertile, well-drained soil; Sam Oldham is an old-fashioned reflex exhibition type grown as a disbudded stem for show-size blooms.

directions: Sam Oldham is a heritage reflex-type exhibition chrysanthemum bearing sizable, long-lasting crimson blooms built from layered, downward-sweeping florets. Fertilize every two weeks from midsummer until the buds show color, and stop pinching by midsummer so the plant channels its remaining growth into finishing its flowers ahead of fall frost. Divide every couple of years to renew vigor, and where winters are severe lift and store the crowns after cutting the top growth back, since this class is traditionally kept going from year to year through division or fresh cuttings rather than left as an undisturbed clump.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Chrysanthemum Classification Guide
Western Australian Chrysanthemum Society — Register of Chrysanthemum Cultivars

common_name: Perry's Peach Chrysanthemum (Single Apricot-Peach Korean Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish before the fall bloom flush; Perry's Peach is part of the same English rubellum breeding line as Mary Stoker and Clara Curtis.

directions: Perry's Peach is a single-flowered Chrysanthemum x rubellum selection bearing lightly honey-scented, soft apricot-peach daisies that start richly colored and fade gently as each bloom ages. It flowers in the typical rubellum window of September into October, forming a clump-forming garden perennial rather than a disposable florist pot mum. Pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to build bushy, self-supporting growth, and divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Chrysanthemum 'Perry's Peach' Plant Profile

common_name: Cathy's Rust Chrysanthemum (Semi-Double Rust-Red Garden Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish before the fall bloom flush; Cathy's Rust is a cold-hardy garden mum selection rather than a disposable florist pot mum.

directions: Cathy's Rust bears semi-double, russet-red flowers in dense clusters over a reliably winter-hardy clump, blooming from late summer through frost when many other perennials are finished. Its aromatic foliage is generally left alone by deer and rabbits, and the flowers draw bees and butterflies during the fall nectar dearth. Pinch stem tips from late spring through early-to-mid summer to build a compact, floriferous plant, and divide every two to three years in spring to prevent the center of the clump from thinning out.

common_name: Weston's Tyler Chrysanthemum (Nearly White Korean Mum)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish before the fall bloom flush; Tyler is grown in New England nursery trade alongside other Korean-type hardy mums such as Sheffield and Venus.

directions: Weston's Tyler is a Korean-type hardy garden mum valued for its nearly white single-to-semi-double daisy flowers, a cooler, cleaner counterpart to the shell-pink Sheffield and lavender Venus cultivars it is often sold alongside. Like other Korean mums, it grows into a shrubby, multi-stemmed clump over the growing season and does not open its flowers until relatively late, holding color well into fall once established. Pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to keep growth dense and self-supporting, and divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: Weston Nurseries — Truly Hardy Garden Mums

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish before the fall bloom flush; Overture forms a wide mound rather than an upright clump.

directions: Overture is a compact, cold-tolerant garden mum with single daisy flowers that open bold red around a bright yellow button center and gradually fade to a multi-toned terracotta as they age, giving each plant a two-color effect late in the bloom cycle. Its mounding habit grows noticeably wider than it is tall, making it useful for filling border edges and large containers without staking. Give it full sun and fertile, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter, and divide crowded clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the mound dense and floriferous.

common_name: Red October Chrysanthemum (Red Korean Mum with Yellow Center)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in early spring so roots establish before the fall bloom flush; Red October is grown and sold alongside other named Korean mum selections such as Sheffield and Mei-Kyo.

directions: Red October is a Korean-type hardy garden mum carrying red flowers centered on a bright yellow eye, giving a warmer, more contrasty look than the pink- and lavender-flowered Korean cultivars it is commonly grouped with. Like other Korean mums it builds into a shrubby, multi-stemmed clump through the growing season and opens its flowers relatively late, holding its color well into fall once nights turn cool. Pinch stem tips through late spring and early summer to encourage dense, self-supporting growth, and divide clumps every two to three years in spring to keep the planting vigorous.
sources: Weston Nurseries — Truly Hardy Garden Mums
